comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: FWA is the weak spot in that thesis though. it's capacity-limited per sector, which is why T-Mobile rations new home internet signups by address, so it can't absorb every cable refugee.

replies.author: constructiontimeagnn
replies.body:
Fair point on the mechanics of sector capacity—you’re 100% right that FWA relies on fallow capacity and address eligibility checks so home internet traffic doesn't degrade high-ARPU mobile phone QoS. 

However, that constraint doesn't break the thesis for three structural reasons:

1. The Math of Market Share:  
The U.S. has \~125M+ broadband households. T-Mobile’s long-term target is 15M FWA subscribers by 2030 (up from \~7M+). That is only \~12% total market share. T-Mobile doesn't need to absorb "every" cable refugee; capturing just 1 out of 8 households nationwide fully satisfies the model across their 80,000+ macro sites.

2. The Convergence Model (FWA + Fiber JVs):  
FWA isn't working in a silo. Where cell sectors hit capacity ceilings in dense suburban corridors, T-Mobile is deploying off-balance-sheet fiber JVs (Lumos and Metronet). Management has guided to 12M–15M fiber passings and 3M–4M FTTH customers by 2030, bringing total broadband to 18M–19M. Fiber offloads the dense clusters; FWA sweeps up the rest.

3. Expanding Spectrum Depth:  
Capacity isn't static. T-Mobile continues lighting up C-band, 3.45 GHz, and 2.5 GHz Auction 108 spectrum, paired with 5G SA 4-carrier aggregation (4xCA) and 64T64R Massive MIMO. That continuously widens sector throughput.

Bottom line: Cable operates high-fixed-cost networks. Charter and Comcast don't need to lose 100% of their base to bleed; losing 1-2% of high-margin broadband subs annually destroys their operating leverage. Meanwhile, every incremental FWA sub on T-Mobile’s fallow capacity drops at \~80% flow-through margins with near-zero CapEx.

replies.author: constructiontimeagnn
replies.body:
The reason 12M–15M passings by 2030 works is because of the baton pass:

1. Perfect Timing Synergy:  
FWA doesn't need fiber to bail it out today; FWA is already printing 400k+ net adds a quarter on fallow spectrum with near-zero CapEx. The fiber JV passings (Lumos/Metronet) ramp up precisely between 2026–2028, right as the densest suburban cell sectors hit their FWA quotas. It’s an engineered transition.

2. The Speed Reality:  
Adding 12M–15M passings in \~4 years via off-balance-sheet JVs is lightspeed compared to legacy telecom. AT&T took a decade and bloated its balance sheet with $100B+ in debt to trench fiber. TMUS is getting the passings with 20%+ target IRRs and zero debt overhang.

3. The Multiple Isn't Stretched:  
People see a \~15x forward P/E and compare it to AT&T/Verizon at 8x–9x. But T and VZ trade at single-digit multiples because their top lines are stagnant and they carry massive debt loads. 

TMUS trades at 15x while:  
• Growing FCF to $18B–$20B+ (8%–10% CAGR)  
• Retiring \~5% of its share float every year through buybacks  
• Invading Enterprise (Chris Sambar) and Rural (scaling past 24% toward 30%+)  
• Crushing SG&A via IntentCX

At 15x forward earnings with double-digit EPS growth and a rising dividend, it’s not pricing in 2030 perfection—it’s pricing in dominant compounding execution.
